welcome.eyebrow: NKU AI DAY · COMPUTER VISION LAB
welcome.headline: Can the AI tell what it’s looking at?
welcome.body: Choose any available trained rock, point your phone at it, and see whether the AI recognizes which object you are holding. Then reflect on whether that kind of computer vision interaction would improve a museum experience.

privacy.body: Camera images stay on your device. Anonymous interaction results and feedback are recorded for this prototype study.

discover.title: Recognition is a testable claim.
discover.text: You trained the AI with multiple photos of this exact rock. The live camera test checks whether those examples are enough for the model to recognize the physical object from a new view.
discover.uncertainty: Today’s model is a prototype. A successful recognition is useful evidence about the interaction, but it does not mean the model is production-ready for museum use.

finale.headline: Now think like a museum visitor.

about.headline: What are we learning for Cincinnati Museum Center?
about.intro: This Computer Vision Lab uses test objects from a personal collection—not Cincinnati Museum Center artifacts. The goal is to let students experience object recognition firsthand while generating evidence for the CMC project.
about.section1Body: Can a model recognize which of several trained physical objects a visitor is holding from a live phone camera view? Tomorrow’s lab uses multiple proxy objects so more students can participate without waiting for a single specimen.
about.section2Body: If recognition works, does it actually improve the experience? Does it help people engage with the physical object, or does the technology create confusion and friction?
about.section3Body: The field study helps the AI Native Studio compare computer vision with simpler alternatives such as QR codes or manual object selection before recommending what belongs in the final museum experience.
